section.title: James Cowling: Dropbox Storage, Simple Systems, and Engineering Careers in the AI Era
section.deck: James Cowling, former most senior engineer at Dropbox and now CTO of Convex, argues that simple systems, clear purpose, and daily mental effort matter more than complexity, promotion chasing, or AI hype.

blocks.text: James Cowling, introduced as formerly the most senior engineer at Dropbox and now CTO of Convex, argues that good engineering starts from a deep understanding of why something is being built. From that he draws several connected claims. Simple systems are harder to design than complex ones. Teams should be organised around the problem they solve, not the system they own. Leaders should explain purpose instead of relying on authority. Engineers grow by owning consequences and by struggling with hard problems before asking an AI tool. The conversation moves from his distributed-systems PhD, through the Dropbox storage system and its move off S3, to tech leadership, careers in the AI era, and his work at Convex. Everything below is Cowling's own account, opinion or estimate.
blocks.heading: Cowling's view: the best engineering comes from understanding why

blocks.question: What problem was the Granola research solving, and what else was in Cowling's graduate work?
answer: Cowling says his career has followed two threads. One is abstractions: building simple models for complex problems, which he treats as a hard design exercise in how to design APIs. The other is large-scale transactional systems. He calls transactions one of the most incredible abstractions ever invented, because they let engineers manage what he considers probably the hardest problem in computer science, concurrency.

Granola, his PhD work, was an algorithm for coordinating distributed transactions, in particular what he called one-shot transactions. Code is sent to the server to run a set of reads and writes on several nodes, and the system must commit them atomically across shards. His master's thesis was on Byzantine fault tolerance. His best-known graduate paper, Viewstamped Replication Revisited, redefined a protocol that predates Paxos. Cowling regards Paxos, Raft and Viewstamped Replication as basically the same idea. Granola appeared slightly before Spanner, so it earned a citation in the Spanner paper, but attention then moved to Spanner.

followups.question: How does Granola avoid the cost of voting for consensus?
answer: Cowling says people often think about performance as raw horsepower, such as disk and network speed, but nobody has meaningfully faster disks than anyone else. What matters at scale is eliminating points of coordination, so that parallel throughput is not reduced to serial throughput.

In Granola, an independent transaction is one where the participants run pure functions over independent state, so each reaches the same result alone. They only need to agree on the serial order: each proposes a timestamp and the maximum is chosen. Most of the paper is about exchanging those timestamps efficiently. The alternative he wanted to avoid is two-phase commit with two-phase locking, which he says is slow because it blocks systems during the transaction, and risky because a node depends on another node returning.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.question: How did Cowling build and test a distributed system as a PhD student at MIT?
answer: Cowling says this was early in the days of AWS. His group had a rack of servers in its office, and academics could also use PlanetLab, a communal set of nodes that was a free-for-all with continual problems. For a long time he slept next to his desk and woke at odd hours to check whether PlanetLab was free so he could start a benchmark.

He says this was near the point where Google, with affection, ruined systems research. Before then the value of a paper was the idea. Papers then began to arrive from Google, Amazon and others describing whole systems, and program committees began to expect realistic benchmarks that graduate students could not produce. Cowling argues this obscured ideas, and cites the old paper on leases, which introduced the time-based lock, as a pure idea paper. He sees much systems research as now industrial, and academia as a great place for impractical work but unable to compete on pragmatism.
blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.question: Looking back, would industry have been a better path than a PhD?
answer: Cowling says many students wrongly see a PhD as college plus plus. In his view it is training to become a researcher, and most people who want to be professional engineers should not do it.

His caveat is that a student at a top program reaches a point where they face a problem no one else, including their advisor, can answer. They cannot read a book or ask ChatGPT, and must learn to think through uncertainty. He believes this is valuable for all engineers, and feels lucky to have done grad school before LLMs offered a crutch. His summary is that researchers should do a PhD and builders should build. In academia the goal is to advance knowledge, in industry it is to solve problems, and he gravitates toward the latter. His later work has been innovative, but the goal was never research.
blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.question: What is multi-homing, and what problem does it solve?
answer: Cowling defines multi-homing as keeping data in two locations, or homes, and separates primary-secondary replication from active-active multi-homing (compared in the table below). He describes Dropbox's block storage as truly multi-region, so that a whole region such as Ashburn, Virginia could go down with zero downtime and the data still safe.

He says multi-homing appeals to many engineers but is not right for most companies, because the speed of light is fixed. He estimates a synchronous write across US regions adds around 60 milliseconds to the commit path, which most applications cannot tolerate. When teams ask him about active-active, he normally says not to. If US East is down for a day the company is down, which is a shame, but avoiding the complexity lets a team move faster and build a better product. He sees multi-region availability as making sense for a company like Dropbox, with several exabytes and hundreds of millions of customers.

followups.question: How many replicas would Dropbox keep of a single document?
answer: Cowling says it is many. Dropbox advertised at least 12 nines of durability, and the internal model put it around 24 nines, which by the model means the universe would end before data is lost. This is his recollection, not a checked figure.

The method is erasure coding, which combines blocks with an encoding scheme and spreads fragments across locations. At that scale, he says, placement considers racks and rows on different power feeds and different eras and makers of hard drives, because they can fail together. A file might be spread over around 27 fragments, which does not mean 27 times the storage. Dropbox used a custom encoding matrix and fed in variables such as disk cost and network bandwidth cost, since the choice is between more copies and fast re-replication after a failure. He says the complexity was abstracted into one part of the system and did not leak elsewhere.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

followups.question: If a document is split over many machines, how do you avoid waiting on a slow one?
answer: Cowling says erasure coding is actually faster. In a simplified example that is not Dropbox's scheme, if a file can be rebuilt from six of nine fragments, the system asks all nine and returns the data once the first six answer. In practice Dropbox also kept a copy on a single disk for fast access and served data from a region near the user.

He then argues against saving money by leaving the cloud. Almost certainly you cannot, he says, unless your needs are small or fixed or you invest very heavily. Beating Amazon on storage efficiency requires supply chain, capacity and data center teams negotiating with disk makers to push disks to 90 to 95 percent full. He calls the Dropbox effort a ballpark billion-dollar project and, as far as he knows, then the largest data migration in history. In his view the cloud is an incredible innovation and most people should focus on their applications.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.title: Two forms of multi-homing as Cowling describes them
rows: All writes commit authoritatively in one region and are replicated to a second region afterward.
Business continuity. His Dropbox example was staying up if the whole West Coast failed.
A window of vulnerability in which recently written data may be lost.
A write is not reported as successful until it has landed in every region.
Loss of a whole region with zero downtime and no data loss, as in Dropbox's block storage.
Latency in the commit path. He gives about 60 milliseconds across US regions as a rough figure.

blocks.question: Since most people should not run their own storage, why did Dropbox migrate away from S3?
answer: Cowling says leaving S3 was a long-held company desire, from before he joined in 2012. The motive was strategic: to control the company's destiny. Dropbox was then in the file sync and share category, and owning the file system was valuable. He says the project saved a huge amount of money, before the company went public, but was very hard and would be difficult to emulate without a huge investment.

He also sees an organisational benefit in hard problems. They attract engineers who like them, and those engineers rotate to other parts of the system once the problem is solved. After the very small storage team shipped, a colleague named Jamie redesigned the sync protocol and desktop client, and Cowling worked on the file system and distributed databases. His caution is that such a system is like having a baby: you cannot build it and be done, because you must keep investing.

followups.question: Did S3 try to counter-negotiate before Dropbox left?
answer: Cowling says Amazon was not particularly aware for a long time, though data center people noticed Dropbox buying a lot of space. Dropbox already had heavily discounted rates, but at some point Amazon could not match its cost efficiency, because the new system really was more efficient at launch. He gives two reasons: Dropbox used new shingled magnetic recording disks, probably the first at scale, and it understood its own workloads tightly, whereas S3 must be designed for everybody. He would not recommend another company do this now, but it made sense for Dropbox then.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

followups.question: What is an example of workload knowledge letting Dropbox do what S3 could not?
answer: Cowling says a newly uploaded file is accessed quickly, for example when shared or previewed, and access then decays. So Dropbox ran two clusters. One was temporary storage that was cheap to read and write but inefficient to store in. Data landed there first and was moved in bulk in the background to a colder, more static system that used more efficient algorithms and could go down for writes without harm. That separated the live write path from the long-term read path.

He adds a hardware example: estimating the amps each rack's circuit breaker needed from access patterns, and sometimes getting it slightly wrong, so that a bad batch of disks caused extra re-replication and a hot rack. He says this level of tuning only makes sense at multi-exabyte, million-drive scale.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.question: Why did the storage system move from Go to Rust?
answer: Cowling says the prototype was in Python, which he defends as decent for IO but poor for concurrency and memory management and hard to refactor. Because the system had to be correct, the team moved to Go, before Go was generally available. Go suits concurrency and proxies.

At around a million nodes, he says, the team itemised every cost, even sheet metal, and wanted nearly all spending to go on disks. A big problem was how much memory nodes used and how unpredictable it was under the Go runtime. In a storage system an out-of-memory restart looks like a disk failure and triggers re-replication, so a batch of them can cascade. He recalls a band, possibly De La Soul though he is unsure, releasing an album on Dropbox. A load spike on a few files made machines run out of memory, and reconstructing from replicas turned one fire hose of load into roughly seven. That is congestion collapse, and he calls designing against it one of the hardest parts of Magic Pocket, the storage system.

The team switched the storage nodes to Rust, before Rust was generally available, which he calls risky. It also dropped the file system and addressed disks directly using draft specifications from the disk makers. Congestion collapse stopped, reliability improved, and spending shifted almost entirely to disks.

followups.question: Was there a postmortem for the cascading failure?
answer: Cowling says none was needed, because the problem was evident as it happened when he was paged at night. He treats it as an argument for the cloud: you cannot cheaply swap memory chips in every machine of a hardware fleet that cost hundreds of millions.

He recalls a week when two trucks delivering racks both crashed, costing what he thinks was around six weeks of capacity. It was like a laptop disk filling, across a million disks, and customers could not be told to go away. The lesson was to plan buffers and design out congestion collapse and memory spikes. He also describes FMEA, a spreadsheet of every bad thing that could happen and how bad it would be, a kind of pre-mortem, and says he likes the moments where the rubber hits the road and no one can help.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

followups.question: At Instagram we had DEFCON knobs that degrade a system gracefully. Did Dropbox have something like that?
answer: Cowling says never for durability, which was absolutely non-negotiable. There were knobs for background processes, CPU and memory, so a load spike could be met by turning off background work and test load. The team also built a system called trampoline: if capacity got too close to a threshold, data was written to S3, possibly around 30 petabytes in the worst case, and moved back later. That saved money because capacity could run closer to the edge. It rarely happened outside tests, but he found the escape hatch reassuring.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.question: How do you coordinate such a large migration without breaking the system while it runs?
answer: Cowling says the first builders were a handful of engineers, perhaps three to six. His first answer is to keep things simple, with cleanly abstracted systems whose failure modes are understandable and which are decoupled. He adds that in his view agents are not good at building simple systems, so simplicity is still a human domain for now.

His second answer is thick validation. During the move off S3 the team did a dark launch, double-writing data to both systems. The founders required six months with no incidents, downtime or data loss before any data could be deleted from S3. Partway through, a bug slipped through several layers of release process into production. Nothing bad happened, but Cowling told the VP the clock would reset, at a cost he describes as double-digit millions. The VP thanked him and said they trusted him. Cowling says people were almost proud, since he was acting on the company's principle of putting user safety first.

Once validators were running around the clock, the team migrated as fast as it could, peaking at about 764 gigabits per second between Amazon and Dropbox. He received a slightly nasty email from someone at Amazon about doing so many reads and so few writes, and did not reply. He stresses that AWS was a great partner and Dropbox still uses it, but says the episode probably strained the relationship.

followups.question: You mentioned simplicity. Is there a concrete example?
answer: Cowling describes the map from each block to the disks that hold it. Dropbox used a cluster of about a thousand MySQL nodes indexed by block ID. New hires from academia or elsewhere called it unsophisticated and suggested a Patricia trie or a distributed hash table. He says that optimises for the wrong thing. With one big table, services can walk it constantly and check that every block is where it should be; a complex structure is much harder to validate. Design should be for validation and understanding, because what matters is what you do when a system does not work.

He argues that engineers who want to look like intellectual problem solvers drift toward complexity, whereas simple systems are far harder to design. The best compliment is for people to call a design the obvious way, as they say of Convex, though it was not obvious when no one else was doing it. Simplicity scales over years as well as queries per second: a simple system can absorb new features and changed requirements for five years, while a complex over-optimised one cannot. He warns that, especially with LLM-assisted design, something working does not make it maintainable or understandable.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.question: Engineers I know have had promotions rejected because their work was not complex enough. What do you make of incentives that reward complexity?
answer: Cowling says it nearly angers him and is partly why he started his own company. His ideal is to be appreciated for solving the problem. He uses a farming analogy: there was no incentive to make milking a cow complicated, because the reward was milk. A startup works the same way. At a large company, with many layers, people build alternative incentives such as green checks on an OKR plan, and he finds it maddening when people chase artificial goals. He accepts some people have no choice, but says working where you are appreciated for problem solving makes you a much better engineer.

From interviewing, he says some engineers at big companies, with Google as his example, describe building a system but cannot say why or how it is used, only that a VP asked. He calls this a caricature, and says it allows competent engineering but the best engineering comes from a deep understanding of why. At Convex everything exists for a reason; you should not build a fancy load balancer unless needed, though he notes the team now does need one.

To cynical juniors he says to fight the system a little. His happiest times were spent dedicating himself to a cause and trusting that promotion would follow, or he would go elsewhere. He suggests finding a team that wants to do good work, which he calls being true to yourself, not selling out.
blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.question: Your writing on system bias argues for orienting teams around missions, not systems. How do you do that?
answer: Cowling says one of his least fun but most impactful jobs at Dropbox was shutting down projects, such as one with 60 people working for two years that did not seem to make sense. In private the team often doubted it too, but inertia and fear of trouble kept them going. He tells a story about the storage team. While building the system it was called the Magic Pocket team, after a silly code name. As soon as it shipped, he renamed it the storage team, which took real work across emails, channels and repositories.

His argument was that the storage team's job is to meet the organisation's storage needs, not to advocate for Magic Pocket. If moving back to S3 were better, the storage team should be the one to say so. A team named for the system would find that threatening to its identity and career, but a storage team would see a new product. He says it sounds like a silly management philosophy, but a team's identity should be built around solving a problem, not defending a system.

followups.question: If inertia is so strong, how did you fight it and close those projects?
answer: Cowling credits some luck. He was there early and worked 16-hour days, which he does not recommend, and people saw that he cared. That gave him what he calls confidence capital. He was afraid for wrong decisions, not for his career.

When staff-plus engineers he mentored complained about an inefficiency, he asked whether it should be solved right now, and if so what lower priority work should stop. Often nothing was lower priority, and then, he says, you accept it. He sums it up as you break it, you bought it. Shutting a product meant redirecting it, not causing problems, and he credits his success to ownership: instead of complaining he wanted to fix things. When infra had seven to nine people, a new hire from Google would say someone must build a logging framework, and he would ask who, since it was only them. Complaining that an idea is dumb does not work, he says, but offering another idea and owning it is a recipe for success.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

followups.question: You asked people whether a project would still be the best use of time. How does that help a tech lead?
answer: Cowling says almost nothing is a yes or no question; it is a question of prioritisation. Redesigning the database may be fine in principle, but if it is not the most important thing now, you do not do it. When people say a VP will not let them do something, he notes the VP probably has different priorities, not that the VP is dumb.

He applies the same view to the career ladder. He disputes that becoming senior means getting better at programming, and says his own peaked around level four. What grew was the scope he cared about. A first-year engineer should not try to redirect company strategy for lack of wisdom, but IC6, 7 and 8 engineers are not necessarily the best programmers; they have broader perspective.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.question: Would you choose doing the wrong thing and getting promoted, or doing the right thing and not being promoted?
answer: Cowling picks the second without hesitation. He calls his argument tacky: above a certain level of skill and seniority, he says, pay is high enough that money stops mattering, so junior engineers over-optimise for promotion and salary when they should invest in themselves. He notes it is easy for an older person to say this.

He says that for a long time Dropbox had no proper level system, and he believes that as tech lead he earned the least on his team, which he knew as a technical manager. It worked out. He would take working with the best people over 20 percent more money. There is no shame in a regular job, he says, but anyone maximising career growth should maximise skills, and he believes talent correlates with pay and growth. His advice to early-career engineers is to land at the best company, with the best people, on the most important problems.

followups.question: Many people face the same incentives and conclude differently. What motivates you to do the right thing when the system does not reward it?
answer: Cowling says the system does reward it, but not visibly at first. People who job-hop less grow the most, he argues: if you do not stay around three years, you do not see whether your decisions were good, and you cannot become a very talented senior engineer without owning their consequences. He compares leaving early to leaving a basketball game before the end. If the job is bad, he says, leave it.

He left academia because he disliked inventing a problem and a solution and then writing a paper to persuade others; he wanted to build and ship and see whether it worked. Readers living paycheck to paycheck may reasonably ignore his advice, he adds. For others, enjoying work every day matters more to quality of life than a fancier car, and he says he loves cars. He and his co-founder can only do work they care about, which he calls a bigger luxury than a first-class flight, and which takes very active effort.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.question: Your profile calls you an occasional manager. How did you decide to dip into management?
answer: Cowling says most people should not want to be managers and he sees too much desire for it as a bit of a red flag. Each time he did it, a team needed a manager. He enjoys accountability and having weight on his shoulders, but returned to engineering whenever someone else could take over.

He calls management educational, because you see that companies and engineers are more complicated than you thought. But he cautions strongly against going in too early, as well-meaning people push it as career advancement. In his view people should generally not manage in their first three years, and ideally should reach staff engineer first, because management before becoming an excellent technician limits later influence on strategy.

followups.question: How does that play out for someone who goes into management too early?
answer: Cowling says they become people managers who see the job as keeping a team happy, coordinating it or handling day-to-day issues, but are not organisational leaders pushing the team toward excellence or shaping technical strategy. He says the best companies have managers who are very technical, since a non-technical manager cannot evaluate the team's work. The host adds that this may feed complaints that a manager does not understand the team, and Cowling suggests a manager may not, if they have not spent enough time developing technical skills.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.question: Tech workers can be anti-authoritarian. How does a tech lead keep credibility?
answer: Cowling says command-and-control companies, where a manager just tells people what to do, are typically not excellent. To get engineers who feel personally responsible for good decisions, they must believe in what the team is doing. As founder and CTO of Convex he cannot just tell someone to do something; they might because they like him, but they would ask why. He spends time explaining where the market is trending and where the product has gaps.

He describes a hierarchy of values, then why, then what, then how. Engineers often debate the how, but he says most organisational conflict comes from well-meaning people who disagree on why: one team thinks the priority is more features to grow, another thinks it is reliability. He wants everyone to have 100 percent alignment on why, and then trusts the team.

At Dropbox one of his jobs was resolving cases where one team called another an idiot. In his telling the other team was not, and once he learned their motivations they chose to do the project, not out of fear. A tech lead has little authority, he says, and leading by authority produces a culture where people do as they are told and good ideas do not arise.

followups.question: Meta technically has no titles. Is Convex run the same way?
answer: Cowling says Convex is very flat but has tech lead roles. He does not fully buy that everyone is just a software engineer; at a company where everyone is a member of technical staff, people still notice when the most senior person comes to their desk. What matters is a culture where no one acts only because a senior person said so. Reputation counts, and an experienced person's explanation probably holds wisdom, but even the most senior should win hearts and minds. A principal engineer who orders a database deleted without saying why is not empowering, he says; one who offers to talk through where the product is trending is.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

followups.question: Your article is titled “don't lead by example.” Why not?
answer: Cowling says leading by example is passive, and engineers are passive people at the best of times. When he first became a leader he tried to model on-call ownership: first to answer pages, writing the reports, jumping on bugs. The team just saw the lead doing many jobs, and might think it was his job, that he knew how and they did not, or that he liked it. He says he was actually just figuring it out. Leadership, he concludes, means understanding human psychology: act with integrity, but also explain what you expect.

He describes a common path for high-achieving tech leads. They care so much that they review every line and join every decision, become the bottleneck, are told to let go, take their hands off the wheel, and the team falls apart. His alternative is a slider between oversight and accountability. With newcomers you check the work. Over time you dial down oversight and dial up accountability by asking about plans, dates and how they will know it is correct, and saying it is theirs. He has found most people like accountability, so long as the lead still shares responsibility. A tech lead should be developing team members so they can take the lead's job.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.title: Moving someone from oversight to accountability

steps.title: Start with oversight
steps.text: A new or junior engineer has their work checked.

steps.title: Name the project
steps.text: Give the person a specific project instead of silently stepping back.

steps.title: Ask for the plan and the date
steps.text: Cowling's example is asking when it will be done, for instance next Thursday, and what the plan is.

steps.title: Ask how they will know it is correct
steps.text: The person defines how they will check their own work.

steps.title: Make the ownership explicit
steps.text: Tell them it is theirs, while the lead still takes shared responsibility.

steps.title: Stay available
steps.text: Ask them to say if there are issues, and keep developing them so they can take the lead's role.

blocks.caption: Editorial summary of the hand-off Cowling describes. The steps and wording are the editor's paraphrase of his example, not a framework he names.

blocks.question: What if you give someone accountability and they blow it?
answer: Cowling says that is part of growth and it does not always work. He recalls writing about paper cuts: low-stakes decisions where a mistake costs about a week. These are good candidates for giving accountability. If the decision fails, the person feels it, which he says is good as long as they are not demoralised, and they learn from it. What he would not allow is for someone to lose an arm, such as a junior person designing a core replication system. He says one of the arts of being a CTO or tech lead is judging how far to trust someone with ownership, and putting safeguards in place.
blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.question: How do you mentor someone who is already a senior staff or principal engineer?
answer: Cowling says there are two parts. Many senior engineers still share common problems, such as delivering harsh feedback. And at that level there is no single archetype, so each person has to find their own brand. He describes himself as a strategic engineer of collaboration, simplicity and abstraction whose coding fell off a cliff, and others as deep science-and-problem-solving engineers. His mentoring helps people become more spiky in the area that makes them special, and works on the personal side: understanding people and the why.

One thing he tells senior engineers is that you cannot change someone's mind in a meeting. Changing a mind takes processes that do not happen live in front of ten people, and forced agreement only bruises the ego. Meetings are generally not for decisions, he says. State the disagreement and reasons, give enough information, let the person reflect, and return a week later.

He compares the alternative to a capitalist attitude toward interpersonal behaviour, where good intentions do not count if you did not convince anyone. You can be the smartest person in the world, he says, but if you cannot change minds you are kind of useless. At that level, effectiveness includes interpersonal dynamics, because hard problems usually need ten or twenty people working together.
blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.question: Has any career advice you would give changed in the last five years because of agentic tools?
answer: Cowling says his own view has not changed much but the industry's has changed dramatically. He says demand for senior engineers in Silicon Valley is incredible, while it is getting harder for juniors to succeed and grow. In his view LLMs cannot do everything: architecture, simplicity and design remain human work, despite what is said on Twitter, and the labs are desperately hiring senior engineers. Junior tasks are becoming commoditised, which worries him.

He describes wisdom as facts put into practice and then synthesised. People say learning is easier now because ChatGPT can explain two-phase commit or snapshot isolation versus serializability, but he says growth requires wisdom, which comes from synthesis. He remains bullish on young people, and Convex hires hungry juniors. His advice is to train your mind and to ignore claims that knowing less engineering will be an advantage, which he calls ludicrous. Engineering is an intellectual discipline for breaking problems into building blocks, and that takes experience, like lifting weights: light weights, or letting a robot lift the heavy ones, does not make you grow.

He would never tell someone not to use a coding agent, but warns of a passivity trap. Spend time in the intellectual wilderness of struggling with a problem: think of a solution first, then check with an LLM. He says it is getting harder to resist reaching for help, and compares this to his own difficulty reading books after a day of watching videos.

followups.question: A junior might say Claude can already do this work and keeps improving, so why build the skill?
answer: Cowling replies that agents are currently not good at many parts of engineering, such as designing distributed-systems protocols or managing a three-million-line code base, and that the labs are still aggressively hiring engineers. He doubts human ingenuity will stop mattering.

He poses a thought experiment. If AGI arrives in a year, one person has given up on problem solving and just runs 17 coding agents accepting whatever Claude says, while another still wants to understand and think hard. Who is better placed? Engineering, he says, is a way of improving your mental processes. He still does whiteboard coding interviews, and says Anthropic does too; candidates are getting worse at coding, but he knows no better way to evaluate problem solving. He compares it to proving already-proven theorems in a maths degree, where the act improves your mind. Coding and engineering are different, he adds, so he sees a promising role for people in engineering even if not in coding.

Quitting because AGI is coming, and being wrong, means getting off the ride. He calls this a cool time for engineering, hates talk that AI leaves humans no role, and wishes his peers would drop the doomer narrative. Convex was started to make it easier to build cool things, not to eliminate jobs.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.question: Why did you leave Dropbox to build Convex, and what is Convex?
answer: Cowling says Dropbox is a great place, but after eight years, and a while as its most senior engineer, he wanted to grow and do his own thing. He left amicably.

He started Convex before the agentic era, on the view that the main differentiator in a large project is the quality of its abstractions, design and architecture. He thinks the hardest challenge in engineering is distributed state management: storing state reliably and reasoning about it while others modify it concurrently. In his description, Convex is a transactional database whose transactions are written in TypeScript and run as serializable stored procedures, with automatic reactivity so the client sees a consistent view of the server. It is designed to be composable, so application developers can build complex full-stack applications.

Agentic development then helped, he says, because what humans find hard, agents find hard too: large code bases, action at a distance, race conditions across services, and keeping architecture simple over time. Almost everyone using Convex has a coding agent building the front end but needs a back end at a higher level of abstraction than AWS or hosted Postgres.

followups.question: Is Convex a layer of abstraction on top of primitives like AWS?
answer: Cowling says yes, and ties it to making problems go away. He mentions that he watched the host's interview with Barbara Liskov, his grad school advisor, with whom he worked on abstraction and clean designs that minimise complexity. He calls AWS and Postgres fine tools, though he says none of the mainstream databases is that great, but says they do not make problems go away. Convex aims to let developers avoid reasoning about state management, concurrency, scheduling, transactions, polling, data sync and type safety.

He sees engineering history as the abstraction floor rising, from punch cards to operating systems, C, higher-level languages and the cloud. Most people never think about how S3 is implemented, which he calls a successful abstraction. He believes the world is overdue for another one level up, and that people using agents mostly do not want to own a Postgres instance or choose between Kafka and RabbitMQ.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

followups.question: What are you most excited about behind the scenes at Convex?
answer: Cowling calls Convex a new operating system in some respects, with primitives such as queries, mutations, actions and subscriptions, running on its own distributed database that tracks read and write ranges. As workloads grow larger and more performance-sensitive, the team is building a lower-level API for efficient background processes and singletons, with fork-like primitives, which he expects to speed up components such as the workflow system.

He says he still finds Convex very hard and struggles every day. Designing the new API is a problem ChatGPT cannot answer well, because it is innovation. He finds it stressful, tiring and exciting, and encourages engineers to look for work on the edge of liking it and finding it tough.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

followups.question: What does fork mean in a distributed system?
answer: Cowling says live traffic is bound by user interactions, so Convex rarely has scale problems there. The harder scaling is background workloads, such as someone kicking off a million jobs, and scheduling. Many of these would be efficient with a background singleton process.

His simple example is a voting system where each vote is a row and a tally is needed. A table scan, the obvious Postgres approach, does not scale. A better design is a background job that adds up new votes and keeps a tally, sleeping on a condition variable when there are none. Most users will never know such primitives exist, he says, but they enable high-performance scheduling and background aggregation.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.question: What was the most technically stimulating work of your career?
answer: Cowling says some of grad school was stimulating, such as formally modelling consensus protocols and reasoning through them on weekend calls with Barbara Liskov. What he found most stimulating, though, was working on a very large storage system with a team when things were going wrong, where the rubber hits the road. At Convex, he says, that happens daily, for instance when a background compaction process runs into trouble and may need partitioning.

He feels most stimulated when a clear constraint is in front of him. He admits he does not know the definition of engineering, but offers his own: engineering is science with constraints, solving problems under resource limits. He is not interested in constraint-free environments, which he calls art, and the more visceral the constraints, the more fun. He says he has always placed himself on the hardest team owning the hardest problem.
blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.question: How did you become a consultant on the TV show Silicon Valley?
answer: Cowling says he had nothing to do with season one. After the show was picked up, the writers had a storyline that reached a compression algorithm and did not know what came next, so they needed a compression expert. He says that ostensibly meant him, though he thinks he was more a storage expert. The writers came to his office and talked, and he became heavily involved in story ideas.

He says the show cares about technical accuracy more than people would expect, down to what a rack and a wall diagram should look like when characters build a data center at home. Mike Judge, who wrote the show and is also known for Beavis and Butt-Head and Office Space, started as a software engineer, Cowling says, and he thinks at Lockheed. The writers collected real stories from many tech companies, and the characters are based on real people and archetypes, which is why some people find it too accurate to watch.

followups.question: Are there Easter eggs, and was the work paid?
answer: Cowling does not think he can name them, but some stories echo early Dropbox, such as ideas being copied by other companies and meetings that turned out to be a competitor gathering information. On pay, he had to be paid because of a Hollywood union rule, though he would have preferred not to because it complicated his visa. He now has a green card, and says he earned a grand total of $400.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.question: Looking back, is there a regret others can learn from?
answer: Cowling says he underinvested in his personal life. He could have left grad school three or four years in and learned as much, or joined Dropbox two or three years earlier and earned more. He says he does not regret missed chances to co-found companies that might have become worth billions. The cost was a lot of sacrifice: on call his whole career, a laptop almost every day, many skipped dinners, parties and events. People in his life have suffered as a result, though they love him and accept his passion.

He says everyone has to decide how hard to drive their career, because there is a real trade-off. Looking back he would take more vacations and have a more balanced life. He cautions against hustle culture, including 996 hours and performative photos of a laptop in a bar. He says he probably works more than 996 himself, but not as a checkbox, only because he wants to do the work. His summary is to focus on solving problems, work hard and be passionate.

followups.question: Your career shows long hours, on call and fires. How do you wind down?
answer: Cowling says he winds down by building things in a little workshop at home. He repeats that the cool thing is doing important work that people use, not working long hours or boasting about running a coding agent all night.
followups.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.question: Do you have a best technical book recommendation?
answer: Cowling admits he has read almost no technical books. In academia he read a lot of papers. He says reading is great but should be balanced with practice, and that most of his learning has come from doing, since nothing develops an engineer like facing a real problem.
blocks.speaker: James Cowling

blocks.question: If you could give your younger self one piece of advice, what would it be?
answer: Cowling would say it will be okay and not to sweat the small stuff so much, while noting that this is hard for him, since his engineering brand is caring about details and he admires the designer Dieter Rams. He says to ignore stories of 22-year-old billionaires, which he calls not repeatable, not normal and not that healthy. He has been an engineer for several decades and is still learning.

He sees a modern feeling that you must max out your growth in the next three months before AGI arrives, and says that is impossible. You do not need to run 17 agents at once. His advice is to orient your career around learning every day, getting better at what you do, and trying to solve things in the simplest way.

followups.question: On Twitter I see the idea of a permanent underclass if you do not make it in time for AGI. How do you respond?
answer: Cowling does not want to be unsympathetic to people in financial difficulty, but calls the attitude not instructive, since there is little to do with it except feel bad. When someone replies that you can get really good at Claude, he says it is not very hard to use. He forgets which model is latest because it does not matter, and gives the example of Ralph, a loop technique that was the biggest thing on Twitter for about a month and that he no longer hears about.

He calls much of this noise, like tech tabloids, comparable to reading about Beyoncé but as a nerd; you are not growing by it. You can miss a new coding agent and, if it matters next year, just use it. He has not seen a hard skill in using Claude Code or similar tools for someone good at engineering. His closing advice is to watch out for tech tabloidism and keep building real things, and he jokes that people should ignore him on Twitter too.
followups.speaker: James Cowling
